title: Where the silicon ends
kicker: What a GPU limits and what software can change
blurb: Why Hopper cannot run 4-bit math at full speed and Blackwell can, and which GPU limits are carved in silicon rather than code.
description: Hopper has no 4-bit tensor cores and Blackwell does. The film separates what is fixed in silicon from what software can still change. It covers how a GPU runs work, the roofline model, dense tensor formats for NVIDIA and AMD, 4-bit weights on Hopper, native NVFP4 training and the CUDA and ROCm software layer.
takeaways: A tensor core is fixed hardware, reached only through instructions that list the number formats it supports.
Decoding one token at a time is memory bound, while large-batch training is compute bound, and a number format affects each differently.
Four-bit weights on Hopper cut memory traffic about four times, but the multiply still runs in 16 bits.
On Blackwell B200, dense 4-bit peak is twice 8-bit, and on B300 it is three times.
Software can change how many bytes move and how close you get to the roofline, but it cannot raise the roofline.
